extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students of poetics/literary theory, and dramatic critics
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating tragic drama: principles for composing plot, character, language, and spectacle so as to produce tragic effect (pity and fear) and a unified whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: the object imitated is an action (not merely character or narration); language should be artistically adorned (rhythm, harmony, song in separate parts). The intended emotional result is catharsis—purgation of pity and fear. This definition frames all other criteria (plot, character, thought, diction, song, spectacle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between Epic and Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry imitates in verse of characters of a higher type and is narrative in form; it admits but one kind of metre and has no limits of time. Tragedy, though similar, is narrative in the form of action and aims (as far as possible) to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: tragic action should be bounded in time (unity of time ideally), whereas epic can be expansive; epic’s narrative scope and metre differ from tragic dramatic enactment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality: Plot, Character, Thought, Diction, Song, Spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle also classifies these: two (Song and Diction) constitute the medium of imitation, one (Spectacle) the manner, and three (Plot, Character, Thought) the objects of imitation. When evaluating or composing, ensure each part is present and serves the whole, though they differ in artistic priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the imitation of the action—by plot I mean the arrangement of the incidents. The Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot (arrangement and causal sequencing of incidents) is the chief determinant of tragic power; a well-constructed plot can outweigh deficiencies in diction or character. Compose scenes so incidents follow by necessity or probability; the end (purpose) of the tragedy depends on plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of Character
rubrics_metrics.description: By Character I mean that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents. Character reveals moral purpose, showing what a person chooses or avoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character is second in importance to plot. Speeches and actions should manifest choices that make moral purpose visible; mere fine diction without revealing choice is not expressive of character. Character is subsidiary—use it to serve the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; it is found where something is proved to be or not to be, or a general maxim is enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought is third in order; in oratory it corresponds to rhetoric. Use Thought to articulate conclusions, arguments, and general truths that advance the plot or reveal character decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (lexis) is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same both in verse and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction includes metrical arrangement and choice of words. It embellishes and clarifies meaning but is subordinate to plot and character. Parts of the play should use diction appropriate to their function (some parts verse-only, some with song).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of Song
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the remaining elements Song holds the chief place among the embellishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song (choral or musical elements) is an embellishment that enhances the emotional and artistic effect; it occupies distinct parts of the play and should be used to heighten rather than substitute for plot-driven action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (opsis) is part of Tragedy—spectacular equipment will be a part of Tragedy—but of all the parts it is the least artistic and connected least with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle has emotional attraction but depends more on stagecraft than on the poet’s art. Do not rely on spectacle to create the tragic effect; it should complement a strong plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeness: beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end. A beginning does not itself follow anything by causal necessity; an end naturally follows some other thing and has nothing following it; a middle follows something as some other thing follows it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must conform to these principles: beginnings, middles, and ends should arise from causal necessity/probability so the action feels complete. When assessing structure, check that events are placed so that they follow logically and produce a cohesive progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude (length) of the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful object (including a plot) must be of a certain magnitude: not too small (confused in an instant) nor too large (eye cannot take it all in). Proper magnitude is comprised within limits so the sequence of events that admit of a change from good fortune to bad or vice versa can be embraced by memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a scope that the audience can grasp in a single view/memory; avoid sprawling action that dilutes unity. Length constraints relating to theatrical competition (e.g., water-clock) are external—focus on artistic limits defined by unity and perspicuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic unity of plot (necessity of parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must imitate one action and be a whole, 'the structural union of the parts being such that, if any one of them is displaced or removed, the whole will be disjointed and disturbed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each scene/incident by whether its removal would visibly affect the whole. Avoid superfluous episodes; every incident should contribute causally or probabilistically to the action’s outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of action over character
rubrics_metrics.description: Action is not with a view to the representation of character: character comes in as subsidiary to the actions. Hence the incidents and the plot are the end of a tragedy; and the end is the chief thing of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging, treat character as a means to drive action rather than an end in itself. Plays that string together admirable character sketches without a coherent plot fail to produce the essential tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry aims at the universal (what may happen)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet relates what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity (the universal), whereas the historian relates what has happened (the particular). Poetry is more philosophical and higher than history because it expresses the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents that exemplify types and universal human responses rather than merely recounting particular historical facts; universality supports dramatic credibility and emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic (epeisodic) plots are faulty
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot is 'epeisodic' in which the episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence. Of all plots and actions the epeisodic are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: episodes linked merely for show or convenience (often to please players or competitions) break natural continuity. Avoid concatenating set-pieces without causal or probable links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise plus causal sequence heightens tragic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that inspire fear or pity are best produced when they come on us by surprise and, at the same time, follow as cause and effect. The tragic 'wonder' is greater when events seem due to design rather than mere chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct reversals/recognitions so they both surprise the audience and are revealed as the necessary or probable consequence of prior incidents; coincidences should have an air of design grounded in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple versus Complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple action: change of fortune takes place without Reversal of the Situation and without Recognition. Complex action: change is accompanied by Reversal, Recognition, or both; these should arise from the internal structure of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with peripeteia and/or anagnorisis) are superior for producing pity and fear. When evaluating, check whether reversals/recognitions are internally motivated rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of the Situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject always to probability or necessity (example: in Oedipus the messenger comes to cheer Oedipus but by revealing identity produces the opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal should be believable as the result of preceding incidents; it should alter the direction of the action and thereby contribute to catharsis. Avoid reversals that are implausible or unmotivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune. The best form of recognition is coincident with a Reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recognitions to be logically tied to earlier clues and causes; when combined with reversal they maximize pity and fear. Recognition may be of persons, deeds, or even trivial tokens, but should be integral to the plot’s causal anatomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversals/Recognitions must be internally caused
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal and Recognition should arise from the internal structure of the plot so that what follows is the necessary or probable result of preceding action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid devices that impose reversals/recognitions from outside the plot’s logic. The best effects arise when revelations and turnabouts are emergent consequences of established causal relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's role: maker of plots rather than versifier
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet or 'maker' should be the maker of plots rather than of verses; since he is a poet because he imitates, and what he imitates are actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plot-construction skills; verse and rhetorical flourishes should serve the plot rather than substitute for it. Even historical subjects can be poetic when they exemplify the probable/universal.
